```{r}
#| message: false
# libraries:
library(Hmisc)
library(mice)
library(tidyverse)
```

The data can be downloaded in xpt form from <https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/continuousnhanes/default.aspx?BeginYear=2015>.

```{r}
#| message: false
# read data:
d1 <- sasxport.get("../data/DEMO_I.xpt")
d2 <- sasxport.get("../data/BPX_I.xpt")
d3 <- sasxport.get("../data/BMX_I.xpt")
d4 <- sasxport.get("../data/GHB_I.xpt")
d5 <- sasxport.get("../data/TCHOL_I.xpt")
d1.t <- subset(d1,select=c("seqn", "riagendr", "ridageyr"))
d2.t <- subset(d2,select=c("seqn", "bpxsy1"))
d3.t <- subset(d3,select=c("seqn", "bmxbmi"))
d4.t <- subset(d4,select=c("seqn", "lbxgh"))
d5.t <- subset(d5,select=c("seqn", "lbdtcsi"))
d <- merge(d1.t, d2.t)
d <- merge(d, d3.t)
d <- merge(d, d4.t)
d <- merge(d, d5.t)
```

```{r}
# rename variables:
# RIAGENDR - Gender
# RIDAGEYR - Age in years at screening
# BPXSY1 - Systolic: Blood pres (1st rdg) mm Hg
# BMXBMI - Body Mass Index (kg/m**2)
# LBDTCSI - Total Cholesterol (mmol/L)
# LBXGH - Glycohemoglobin (%)
d$age <- d$ridageyr
d$sex <- d$riagendr
d$bp <- d$bpxsy1
d$bmi <- d$bmxbmi
d$HbA1C <- d$lbxgh
d$chol <- d$lbdtcsi
d$age[d$age<18] <- NA
```

```{r}
# select complete cases:
dc <- cc(subset(d, select = c("age", "sex", "bmi", "HbA1C", "bp")))
```

```{r}
# analysis:

lm_nobmi <- lm(bp ~ HbA1C + age + as.factor(sex), data = dc)
summary(lm_nobmi)
confint(lm_nobmi)

lm_bmi <- lm(bp ~ HbA1C + bmi + age + as.factor(sex), data = dc)
summary(lm_bmi)
confint(lm_bmi)
```

```{r}
# simulation of measurement error:
ref <- lm_bmi$coef[2]
n.sim <- 1e3
perc.me.exp <- seq(0, .5, .1)
perc.me.conf<- seq(0, .5, .1)
scenarios <- expand.grid(perc.me.exp, perc.me.conf)
var.exp <- var(dc$HbA1C)
var.conf <- var(dc$bmi)
n <- dim(dc)[1]
beta.hat <- matrix(ncol=dim(scenarios)[1], nrow=n.sim)

for (k in 1:n.sim){
  set.seed(k)
  for (i in 1:dim(scenarios)[1]){
    var.me.exp <- var.exp*scenarios[i,1]/(1-scenarios[i,1])
    var.me.conf <- var.conf*scenarios[i,2]/(1-scenarios[i,2])
    dc$HbA1C.me <- dc$HbA1C + rnorm(dim(dc)[1], 0, sqrt(var.me.exp) )
    dc$bmi.me <- dc$bmi + rnorm(dim(dc)[1], 0, sqrt(var.me.conf) )
    beta.hat[k,i] <- lm(bp ~ HbA1C.me + age + bmi.me + as.factor(sex), 
                        data = dc
                        )$coef[2]
  }}
```

```{r}
# create figure:
tot.mat <- cbind(100*scenarios, apply(beta.hat, 2, mean))
colnames(tot.mat) <- c("me.exp", "me.conf", "estimate")

FIGURE <- ggplot(tot.mat, aes(me.exp, me.conf)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", aes(fill = estimate)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(estimate, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#D55E00", mid = "white", high = "#56B4E9", 
                       midpoint = ref) +
  labs(x = paste("% of total variance of HbA1c due to measurement error"),
       y = paste("% of total variance of BMI due to measurement error")) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = unique(tot.mat[,1])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(tot.mat[,1])) +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = "grey"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10))
FIGURE
ggsave("../results/Figure_STRATOS.tif")
```

In the plot of the simulation results we can see that the higher the percentage of BMI variance due to measurement error, the higher the estimated regression coefficient for HbA1c when predicting blood pressure (along with the predictors age, BMI and sex). And the higher the percentage of HbA1c variance due to measurement error (ME), the *lower* the estimated regression coefficient for HbA1c itself. The impact of ME in HbA1c on its coefficient makes sense, because this extra noise is independent of BMI, so their correlation weakens, reducing the coefficient. The fact that the coefficient increases as a result of higher percentages of ME in BMI suggests that there might be some multicollinearity with the effects of BMI and HbA1c, as increasing noise in BMI increases the effect attributed to HbA1c. The shared information (the variance in BP that both are related to) that is otherwise accounted for by BMI then gets attributed to HbA1c. The coefficient changes quite a lot depending on these percentages of ME, from as low as `r round(min(tot.mat$estimate), 2)` with 50% on HbA1c itself and 0% on BMI, to as high as `r round(max(tot.mat$estimate), 2)` with these percentages switched. The coefficients found for HbA1c (and likely for BMI as well) seem to be highly dependent on the quality and precision of measurement of both HbA1c and BMI.
